title: The Sectional Stratospheric Sulfate Aerosol module (S3A-v1) within the LMDZ general circulation model: description and evaluation against stratospheric aerosol observations
abstract: Abstract. Stratospheric aerosols play an important role in the climate system by affecting the Earth's radiative budget as well as atmospheric chemistry, and the capabilities to simulate them interactively within global models are continuously improving. It is important to represent accurately both aerosol microphysical and atmospheric dynamical processes because together they affect the size distribution and the residence time of the aerosol particles in the stratosphere. The newly developed LMDZ-S3A model presented in this article uses a sectional approach for sulfate particles in the stratosphere and includes the relevant microphysical processes. It allows full interaction between aerosol radiative effects (e.g. radiative heating) and atmospheric dynamics, including e.g. an internally generated quasi-biennial oscillation (QBO) in the stratosphere. Sulfur chemistry is semi-prescribed via climatological lifetimes. LMDZ-S3A reasonably reproduces aerosol observations in periods of low (background) and high (volcanic) stratospheric sulfate loading, but tends to overestimate the number of small particles and to underestimate the number of large particles. Thus, it may serve as a tool to study the climate impacts of volcanic eruptions, as well as the deliberate anthropogenic injection of aerosols into the stratosphere, which has been proposed as a method of geoengineering to abate global warming.
problem: Accurately simulating stratospheric aerosols is challenging because their lifetime and radiative properties are critically dependent on the particle size distribution, which is shaped by computationally expensive interactions between aerosol microphysics and atmospheric dynamics that many models struggle to represent without simplification.
method: The paper presents a new sectional stratospheric sulfate aerosol module (S3A-v1) for the LMDZ general circulation model, which simulates the aerosol size distribution and its evolution by representing key microphysical processes like nucleation, condensation, coagulation, and sedimentation.
task: The task is to describe the newly developed Sectional Stratospheric Sulfate Aerosol module (S3A-v1) within the LMDZ general circulation model and evaluate its performance by comparing simulation results against stratospheric aerosol observations during background and volcanic conditions.
innovation: This paper presents the new Sectional Stratospheric Sulfate Aerosol module (S3A-v1) within the LMDZ general circulation model, which interactively simulates sulfate aerosol microphysics and radiative effects to serve as a tool for studying the climate impacts of volcanic eruptions and geoengineering.

The S3A module in the configuration introduced here represents the stratospheric aerosol size distribution with NB = 36 size bins of sulfate particles, with a dry radius ranging from 1 nm to 3.3 µm (i.e. r1 = 1 nm and rn = 3.3 µm for particles at 293 K consisting of 100 % H2SO4) and particle volume doubling between successive bins (i.e. RV = Vk+1/Vk = r 3 k+1/r 3 k = 2 for 1 ≤ k < NB). The number of size bins NB and the corresponding value of RV represent a compromise between the accuracy of the scheme, which increases with higher resolution in size, and the computational cost of the model.

Aerosol amount in each of the size bins is treated as a separate tracer for atmospheric transport in the unit of particle number per unit mass of air as required by our mass-flux scheme (Hourdin and Armengaud, 1999).

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: The formation rate of new particles via binary homogeneous nucleation of sulfuric acid and water vapour is parametrised as a function of the sulfuric acid gas-phase concentration, the relative humidity, and the absolute temperature as described by Vehkamäki et al. As both processes, nucleation and condensation, consume H2SO4 vapour while having very different effects on the particle size distribution, the competition between the two processes has to be handled carefully in a numerical model. Furthermore, this has to be done at an affordable numerical cost, as we aim to perform long global simulations. We address this in the S3A module using an adaptive sub-timestepping.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: The growing of sulfate particles through coagulation is represented through the semi-implicit, volume-conserving numerical scheme described in Jacobson et al. (1994).
We restricted the coagulation kernel to its main component only, i.e. Brownian motion.
